lessons.t: The Preacher Is First a Recipient of Grace

key.x: Pay attention to yourself and to your teaching. Continue in these things, for in doing this you will save both yourself and those who hear you.

lessons.big: The message from the pulpit is fruit grown from the life below the pulpit. Life first, then relationships, then ministry.

secs.h: 1. Paul's Order: Yourself First, Then Your Teaching
p: Paul told Timothy to “pay attention to yourself and to your teaching.” The order is clear: first “yourself,” then “your teaching.” This is not a figure of speech but a spiritual law. A tree must have life before it bears fruit; a preacher must first be changed by God's Word before he can use God's Word to change others.

Many people begin learning to preach by asking, “How do I write an outline? How do I sound good?” These matter, but they are not the starting point. A house needs a foundation first. The foundation is unseen, yet it decides how high the house can rise. The preacher's life is the foundation of the sermon.

secs.h: 2. The Pipe: God's Word Must Flow Through Me First
p: A preacher is like a water pipe. Living water flows from God, through us, to the listeners. The pipe does not produce the water, but if the pipe is dirty, the water that comes out will taste of rust. So God cleanses us first, so that the words flowing out are clean, sweet and full of life.

That is why, when we prepare a sermon, the first listener is not the congregation but ourselves. When you are first pierced, first repent, first give thanks and first obey as you read, your words carry weight on Sunday, because they are grace you have tasted yourself.

secs.h: 3. Five Layers of Change, From the Inside Out
p: The 321 vision teaches us that a changed mindset changes a life, and a changed life changes how we live. The preacher must first go through the five layers of change: mindset, life, lifestyle, relationships and ministry. Ministry is the outermost ring, and it is the last to bear fruit.

If a person's mindset has not been renewed by God's Word, his life is not filled with Christ, and his daily life and relationships are in disarray, then no matter how eloquent he is in the pulpit, he has become “sounding brass or a clanging cymbal.” But when a life has been won by the Lord, even plain words will be used by the Holy Spirit.

secs.h: 4. The Call Is Grace, Not a Qualification
p: We stand in the pulpit not because we are better than others, but because of God's grace. Paul called himself the sinner “of whom I am chief,” yet he received mercy. The greatest danger for a preacher is to treat grace as a qualification and the pulpit as a stage.

When you remember that you are a sinner who has received grace, you will not lecture people from above. You will be like one beggar telling another beggar where to find bread. Such preaching has warmth, humility and power.

c321: Three foundations: Jesus is my example — his thirty hidden years in Nazareth came before his three and a half years of public ministry. The Bible is my standard — “pay attention to yourself” is God's command. The Holy Spirit is my guide — only the Spirit can show us our true condition.

Life first, then relationships, then ministry: preaching is ministry, but its root is life and its branches are relationships. Do not sacrifice your relationship with God, your family or your brothers and sisters (people) for the sake of preaching (the task).
act: Every day this week, read a passage for 15 minutes. Do not think about how to preach it; only ask, “Lord, what are you saying to me?”
Write down one thing you recently received from God's Word and have already put into practice, as material for your own testimony.
Ask a spiritual companion (your 2) to pray for your life, and share your weakness honestly.
chk: When was the last time God's Word pierced my heart?
How much of what I preach have I actually lived?
Do I treat the pulpit as an altar of service or as a stage for performance?
Are my relationships with my family and with my brothers and sisters worthy of the word I preach?
disc: Why does Paul say “pay attention to yourself” before “your teaching”?
Have you ever heard a sermon that was not polished but moved you deeply? Why?
Which of the five layers of change (mindset, life, lifestyle, relationships, ministry) most needs the Lord's renewal in your life?
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, you are my example. Work in me first, so that I am changed by your Word before I serve others with it. Let my life be worthy of the message you have entrusted to me, and let all the glory go to you. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray, Amen.

key.x: For we don't preach ourselves, but Christ Jesus as Lord, and ourselves as your servants for Jesus' sake.

lessons.big: The greatest enemy of preaching is not poor speaking but a self that is too big. Without self, Jesus can reign in the pulpit.

secs.h: 1. The Hardest Problem in the Pulpit: Me
p: Preachers often ask in their hearts, “Did they think I preached well? Did I embarrass myself? Will they invite me again?” At the centre of all these questions is “me.” Self-centred preaching focuses on the preacher; self-emptied preaching focuses on Jesus.

Self is the root of humanity's fall. Adam left his place as a man and wanted to be like God. A preacher who uses the pulpit to build his own name commits the same pride: he leaves his place as a servant and grasps a glory that belongs to God alone.

secs.h: 2. John the Baptist: He Must Increase, I Must Decrease
p: John the Baptist was the most popular preacher of his day, and crowds flocked to him. But when Jesus appeared, he said, “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:30). He called himself the friend of the bridegroom, who rejoices greatly at the bridegroom's voice.

A good preacher is like a mirror. People do not look at a mirror to admire the frame but to see the light in it. The plainer and cleaner the frame, the clearer the light. When people leave saying “Jesus is so good” rather than “What a speaker,” that is a successful sermon.

secs.h: 3. Paul's Decision: Only Jesus Christ and Him Crucified
p: When Paul came to Corinth, it was a city that prized rhetoric and philosophy. He could have displayed his learning, but he wrote, “For I determined not to know anything among you except Jesus Christ and him crucified” (1 Corinthians 2:2).

He went on: “My speech and my preaching were not in persuasive words of human wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power, that your faith wouldn't stand in the wisdom of men, but in the power of God” (1 Corinthians 2:4-5). Being without self does not mean having no gifts, but not relying on them; not skipping preparation, but not trusting in it.

secs.h: 4. Without Self Is Not Emptiness but Entering the Infinite
p: Some think that being without self means being timid and afraid to speak. It is the opposite. “It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20). When “I” step back, Christ lives through me; when my limited self is laid down, the limitless Christ speaks through me.

So the self-emptied preacher is actually the boldest, because he is not afraid of failure. Failure only hurts the pride of “me,” and “me” has already been crucified with Christ. Humility overcomes pride; a self-emptied life overcomes Satan.

c321: Two cores: let Jesus be King — the master of the pulpit is Jesus, not the speaker; let Jesus receive all the glory — after preaching, hand the praise over to the Lord.

Pride is leaving our place and grasping power; humility is laying down power and returning to our place. The preacher's place is that of a servant and messenger; authority over the message belongs to the King who sent him.
act: Before you go up, pray a “crown-laying prayer”: hand over to the Lord, one by one, your longing for praise and your fear of criticism.
For one hour after preaching, do not ask anyone for feedback; first give thanks to the Lord.
Go through your sermon and rewrite every self-centred illustration into a testimony that points to Christ.
chk: When I preach, do I care most about God's presence or about people's reactions?
When praised, does my heart float up? When criticised, does it sink?
Does Jesus appear often enough, and with enough weight, in my sermon?
Can I sincerely rejoice when someone else preaches better than I do?
disc: What would John the Baptist's “I must decrease” look like in today's pulpit?
“Without self is not emptiness but entering the infinite” — how do you understand this?
In what form does pride most often appear in the ministry of preaching?
lessons.pray: Lord, I place myself on the altar. Tear down the pride in me that wants to be seen and affirmed. Let me not preach myself but only you. May I decrease and you increase; may I be hidden and you be revealed. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray, Amen.

lessons.t: The Holy Spirit Is My Guide

key.x: The Lord GOD has given me the tongue of those who are taught, that I may know how to sustain with words him who is weary. He awakens morning by morning, he awakens my ear to hear as those who are taught.

lessons.big: First be a learner, then a teacher; first a listening ear, then a taught tongue.

secs.h: 1. The Ear Before the Tongue
p: The order in Isaiah 50 is striking: God first “awakens my ear to hear,” and only then gives “the tongue of those who are taught.” Preaching is first listening, not speaking. Someone who cannot hear God speak cannot speak for God.

Think of a radio station. How clear the broadcast is depends on how clear the signal it receives. Each morning the preacher tunes in before the Lord, receiving the message from heaven, so that on Sunday it can be transmitted clearly.

secs.h: 2. The Spirit Guides Into Truth
p: Jesus promised: “When he, the Spirit of truth, has come, he will guide you into all truth, for he will not speak from himself; but whatever he hears, he will speak” (John 16:13). Even the Spirit does not speak on his own; he speaks what he hears. How much more should a preacher!

Paul said: “We also speak these things, not in words which man's wisdom teaches but which the Holy Spirit teaches, comparing spiritual things with spiritual things” (1 Corinthians 2:13). Human wisdom can organise a message; only the Spirit can give it life.

secs.h: 3. Use Your Heart and Rely on the Spirit, Not Your Head and Yourself
p: When preparing, it is easy to dive into resources, commentaries and online sermons and piece things together with our heads. These tools help, but they are servants, not masters. “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life” (Proverbs 4:23). The Spirit lives in the heart, not in the head. Use your heart and you find joy; use your head and you find worry.

In practice: pray before you study, meditate before you organise. When you receive a passage, do not open the commentary yet. Read it three times quietly before the Lord and ask the Spirit, “What do you want to say to me and to the congregation through this today?” Write down the first prompting. It is often the seed of the message.

secs.h: 4. Discerning the Spirit's Prompting
p: How do you know whether it is the Spirit's prompting or your own idea? There are three tests. First, it agrees with Scripture — the Spirit never contradicts the Bible. Second, it exalts Christ — the Spirit's work is to glorify Jesus (John 16:14). Third, it bears fruit — repentance, faith, hope and love, not condemnation, fear and confusion.
Add to this the confirmation of spiritual companions. In 235 relationships, let mature spiritual parents or co-workers hear what you have received. Iron sharpens iron.

c321: One of the three foundations: the Holy Spirit is my guide. The first step on the path of service is “Spirit” — seeking the Spirit's guidance and prompting.
Among the eight steps for changing a mindset, “information” is followed by “revelation.” However much you read, without the Spirit's revelation it remains information and cannot change a life.
act: This week, for your next sermon, pray quietly for ten minutes each morning before reading, and write down “today's prompting.”
Practise “three readings”: first for the whole picture, second circling the words that touch you, third responding in prayer.
Check what you have received against the three tests: agrees with Scripture, exalts Christ, bears good fruit.
chk: How much of my preparation time is spent in prayer?
Do I look for resources first or seek God first?
Can I say this message was received from the Lord, or did I simply arrange it myself?
disc: Why does Isaiah 50:4 put the “ear” before the “tongue”?
Have you experienced the Spirit suddenly giving you fresh light while preparing or preaching?
How can we use commentaries and online resources while still relying on the Holy Spirit?
lessons.pray: Holy Spirit, awaken my ear each morning so that I may hear as one who is taught. I do not want to speak from myself, but only what you teach. Fill my heart with your prompting, so that I use my heart and rely on you rather than my head and myself. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray, Amen.

lessons.sub: Properly Handling the Word of Truth

key.x: Give diligence to present yourself approved by God, a workman who doesn't need to be ashamed, properly handling the Word of Truth.

lessons.big: Preaching is not borrowing a text to say our own words, but letting the text speak God's words. Ask first what it meant, then what it means today.

secs.h: 1. The Carpenter's Straight Line
p: “Properly handling” carries the sense of “cutting straight,” like a carpenter sawing along a chalk line or a farmer ploughing a straight furrow. The preacher's task is to cut along the line God has drawn, turning neither left nor right, adding nothing of his own and taking nothing away from God's meaning.

The Levites in Ezra's day give us a model: “They read in the book, in the law of God, distinctly; and they gave the sense, so that they understood the reading” (Nehemiah 8:8). Read, explain, help people understand — these are the three movements of expository preaching.

secs.h: 2. Three Steps: Observe, Interpret, Apply
p: Step one, “observe”: what does the text say? Who, when, where, what happened and how? Watch for repeated words, connectives (because, therefore, but), commands and promises. The more careful the observation, the steadier everything that follows.

Step two, “interpret”: what did the text originally mean? Look at the context, the theme of the whole book, the historical background, and let Scripture interpret Scripture. A passage has one original meaning but many applications. Step three, “apply”: how will this truth change our mindset, life, lifestyle, relationships and ministry today?

secs.h: 3. Avoid Three Common Pits
p: The first pit is “proof-texting”: lifting one sentence out of its context, like cutting one line out of a letter until its meaning changes entirely. The second is “fanciful allegory”: forcing a spiritual meaning onto every detail until the text becomes a playground for the preacher's imagination.

The third is “conclusion first, text later”: deciding what you want to say and then finding a verse to endorse it. That makes the Bible serve me instead of me serving the Bible. The Bible is my standard, not my tool.

secs.h: 4. Read the Whole Bible With Christ at the Centre
p: Jesus said, “These are they which testify about me” (John 5:39). On the road to Emmaus, “beginning from Moses and from all the prophets, he explained to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself” (Luke 24:27). Afterwards they said, “Weren't our hearts burning within us while he spoke to us along the way, and while he opened the Scriptures to us?”

Whether we preach from the Old or New Testament, narrative or poetry, we must finally ask: how does this passage point to Christ, show our need of Christ, or find its fulfilment in Christ? Then preaching will not shrink into moralising but will be the proclamation of the gospel.

c321: One of the three foundations: the Bible is my standard. The second step on the path of service is “Understanding” — grasping and obeying the truth of Scripture.
Changing from a human viewpoint to God's viewpoint begins with honestly letting the text speak, not letting our view cover God's view.
act: Choose a passage of no more than ten verses and write at least twenty observations.
For the same passage, write one sentence of “original meaning” and three sentences of “application today.”
Take your most recent sermon and check it for proof-texting, fanciful allegory, or conclusion-first thinking.
chk: Can I state the original meaning of this passage in one sentence?
Have I looked at the context and the theme of the whole book?
Does my sermon finally bring people to Christ?
disc: Why is “observation” the step preachers most easily skip?
Have you heard a verse used out of context? What does it actually mean?
How are the Emmaus disciples' burning hearts connected with Jesus “opening the Scriptures”?
lessons.pray: Father, your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path. Make me a workman who does not need to be ashamed, properly handling the Word of Truth. Do not let my meaning cover yours, and let me see Jesus in every passage. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray, Amen.

lessons.t: From Our View to God's View
lessons.sub: Finding the Big Idea of the Text

key.x: “For my thoughts are not your thoughts, and your ways are not my ways,” says the LORD. “For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways, and my thoughts than your thoughts.”

lessons.big: A sermon has one big idea. Find God's viewpoint in the passage and the whole message gains its soul.

secs.h: 1. One Sermon, One Point
p: Many sermons are like an overstuffed suitcase: everything is in it, yet when you open it you cannot find what you need. A good sermon is like an arrow with a single head; the feathers and shaft exist only to carry that head to the target.

That arrowhead is the “big idea”: one complete sentence that says what the passage says and therefore how we should respond. If you cannot say it in one sentence, the congregation cannot remember it in one sentence.

secs.h: 2. Four Shifts of Viewpoint
p: The 321 vision reminds us that changing our viewpoint changes our mindset. When searching for the big idea, deliberately make four shifts: from a human viewpoint to God's viewpoint; from an earthly viewpoint to a heavenly one; from a temporary viewpoint to an eternal one; from a worldly viewpoint to a godly one.

Take Joseph being sold. The human view is “jealous brothers harm their brother.” God's view is “you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good” (Genesis 50:20). The same passage, seen from another angle, turns a human tragedy into God's plan of salvation.

secs.h: 3. Three Questions to Distil the Big Idea
p: First: what “subject” is this passage about? (For example: faith, humility, forgiveness.) Second: what does the passage “say” about that subject? (For example: God gives grace to the humble.) Third: how does God want us to “respond”? (For example: lay down power and return to our place.)

Combine the answers into one sentence: “Because God gives grace to the humble, we lay down power and return to our place, letting God be God.” That sentence is the north star of your sermon; every section must move toward it.

secs.h: 4. Focus on Jesus
p: The focus is on Jesus — not on ourselves, not on others, not on our circumstances. When the big idea stops at “we must try harder,” the message becomes a burden of law. When it points to “Jesus has accomplished it, therefore we can,” the message becomes the power of the gospel.

As the heavens are higher than the earth, God's thoughts are higher than ours. The preacher's task is to bring heaven's thoughts down to earth, so that in a single message the congregation lifts its eyes from the ground and sees heaven.

c321: Changing your viewpoint changes your mindset; changing your mindset changes your life. The big idea is the hinge of this shift of viewpoint in preaching.
Focus on Jesus: preaching must finally help people see Jesus, not only their problems, other people or their circumstances.
act: Write a big idea of no more than 25 words for your next sermon.
Look at the same passage again through the four shifts of viewpoint and write down the light each one brings.
Read your big idea to a family member and ask them to say it back in their own words, to check that it is clear.
chk: Can I state the big idea of this sermon in one sentence?
Did the big idea come out of the text, or did I add it to the text?
Does it point to “try harder” or to “Jesus”?
disc: Why should a sermon have only one big idea?
Choose a Bible story you know well and try shifting from the human view to God's view.
How does “focus on Jesus” turn preaching from a burden into good news?
lessons.pray: Lord, your thoughts are higher than my thoughts. Open my eyes to see your viewpoint in every passage, to look up from earth to heaven and to see eternity beyond the present. In every message I preach, bring people's focus back to Jesus. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray, Amen.

lessons.t: Building the Skeleton of a Sermon

key.x: Further, because the Preacher was wise, he still taught the people knowledge. Yes, he pondered, sought out, and set in order many proverbs. The Preacher sought to find out acceptable words, and that which was written blamelessly, words of truth.

lessons.big: Good structure is like a skeleton: unseen, yet it holds up the whole body, so listeners can follow, remember and take it home.

secs.h: 1. The Preacher's Method: Ponder, Seek Out, Set in Order
p: The Preacher “pondered, sought out, and set in order,” and “sought to find out acceptable words.” Organising a message is not unspiritual; it is an expression of love for the listeners. God is a God of order: “Let all things be done decently and in order” (1 Corinthians 14:40).

A sermon without structure is like a pile of sand: the preacher is moved, but the congregation gets lost. A structured sermon is like a paved road; people can follow step by step until they arrive where God wants to take them.

secs.h: 2. Three Common Structures
p: “Passage-by-paragraph”: points follow the natural paragraphs of the text — closest to the text and ideal for expository preaching. “Problem and answer”: raise a real-life question, then find the answer in the text — suited to evangelistic or topical messages. “Story progression”: follow the narrative and draw out truth at its turning points — suited to Old Testament stories and the Gospels.
Whichever you choose, every point of the outline must directly support the big idea, like pillars of a house all holding up the same roof.

secs.h: 3. Four Principles for a Good Outline
p: First, parallel: points share the same sentence pattern, for example “God … so we …”. Second, brief: each point under about eight words, memorable after one hearing. Third, ordered: from simple to deep, from inside out, or following the order of the text. Fourth, few: usually two to four points; three are easiest to remember.

An example, “God's Heart in the Book of Jonah”: 1. God pursues the one who runs; 2. God saves the one who repents; 3. God teaches the one who is angry. Three points — parallel, brief, in the order of the text, and all pointing to the big idea of God's mercy.

secs.h: 4. Three Elements Under Each Point: State, Illustrate, Apply
p: Under each main point there can be three elements: “state” — what the text says on this point; “illustrate” — make it clear with a picture or example; “apply” — what it means for us today. Like a body with bone, flesh and blood.

The proportions need not be identical for every point, but if any one is missing, the message loses balance: only stating is too dry, only illustrating is too light, only applying is too heavy. Together they make a living sermon.

c321: The fourth step on the path of service is “Serve”: letting Jesus live and reign in me, serving by his authority and power. Structure is the vessel; the Holy Spirit is the life of its content.
Among the eight steps for changing a mindset, “practise, review, correct, repeat” is exactly how an outline is perfected. Do not be afraid to rewrite.
act: Write outlines in three different structures for your big idea, and choose the clearest.
Trim each point to about eight words and make the sentence patterns parallel.
Under each main point, mark the three elements: state, illustrate, apply.
chk: Does every point directly support the big idea?
Are there too many points? Can listeners remember them after one hearing?
Have I made the structure the star and forgotten to rely on the Spirit?
disc: Do structure and the Spirit's leading conflict? Why or why not?
Which sermon outline do you remember best? Why did it stay with you?
Try writing a three-point outline for Psalm 23.
lessons.pray: God of order, give me wisdom to ponder, seek out and set in order as the Preacher did. Let the structure I prepare be a useful vessel filled with your life and truth, so that the congregation can understand, remember and obey. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray, Amen.

key.x: With many such parables he spoke the word to them, as they were able to hear it.

lessons.big: Truth is the frame; illustrations are the windows. Windows let the light in so people can see what truth looks like.

secs.h: 1. Jesus Is the Best Preacher
p: When Jesus spoke of the kingdom, he did not use abstract theological terms. He spoke of sowing seed, mustard seeds, yeast, a lost sheep and a prodigal son. He spoke the word “as they were able to hear it.” That phrase matters: preaching is not about how deep I can go, but how much they can receive.

A parable is like a bridge. One end rests on the life people know; the other rests on truth they do not yet know. As people step onto the familiar end, they are carried across to the truth without noticing.

secs.h: 2. Four Marks of a Good Illustration
p: First, clear: understood at once, without needing to explain the illustration itself. Second, fitting: it truly illuminates the point rather than being merely a nice story. Third, close to home: drawn from the congregation's life — the kitchen, the office, the phone, the market. Fourth, true: testimonies must be honest, never exaggerated or patched together, and never someone else's experience told as your own.
An illustration is a window, not the house. If it runs too long, people remember the story but forget the truth, like admiring the window frame and missing the view.

secs.h: 3. Where Illustrations Come From
p: From Scripture: illustrations that let Scripture interpret Scripture carry the most authority, such as David and Goliath for faith. From life: carry an “illustration notebook” and jot down what you see, hear and experience. From creation: “For the invisible things of him since the creation of the world are clearly seen, being perceived through the things that are made” (Romans 1:20).

From your own testimony: the most powerful illustration is your own experience of being changed by God. But remember to be without self — the hero of the testimony is Jesus, not me. Say “how the Lord helped me,” not “how spiritual I am.”

secs.h: 4. The Craft of Storytelling
p: A good story has four elements: a person, a situation, a turning point and an outcome. Use concrete detail instead of abstract description. Do not say “he was very sad”; say “he sat in the hospital corridor, phone in hand, and never pressed call.”
After the story, connect it back to the truth in one sentence: “God is like this too…” Do not leave people to guess. When the window is open, point outside and say, “Look — that is the love of God.”

c321: Jesus is my example: he is the master of preaching in parables, and he himself — the Word made flesh — is the ultimate illustration.
Testimony without self: let Jesus receive all the glory. The focus of a testimony is God's grace, not our achievements.
act: Start an “illustration notebook” (or use this app's notes) and record at least five illustrations from life this week.
Give each main point of your sermon an illustration and write the sentence that ties it back to the truth.
Write one of your testimonies in about 200 words and check whether the hero is Jesus or yourself.
chk: Are my illustrations windows, or houses that steal the show?
Are they true and free of exaggeration?
Do I use pictures familiar from the congregation's daily life?
disc: Which of Jesus' parables helps you most? Why?
Share a sermon illustration you still remember.
How can a testimony be told “without self,” so that the Lord is glorified?
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, you open hearts with parables. Open my eyes to see the parables in everyday life, and let my mouth speak your word as people are able to hear it. Let every window let your light shine through, so people see your beauty. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray, Amen.

lessons.sub: Application Through the Five Layers of Change

key.x: But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves.

lessons.big: A sermon without application is like a letter without an address: however beautifully written, it never reaches people's lives.

secs.h: 1. The Mirror
p: James says a hearer who is not a doer “is like a man looking at his natural face in a mirror; for he sees himself, and goes away, and immediately forgets what kind of man he was.” God's Word is a mirror. The goal of preaching is not to have people admire the mirror but to see themselves and set themselves in order.
So every sermon must answer, “So what?” When people wake up on Monday morning after hearing it, what will be different?

secs.h: 2. A Framework: The Five Layers of Change
p: The 321 vision's “five layers of change from the inside out” is the most complete framework for application. Mindset: which thought does this truth renew? Life: which quality of Christ should grow in me? Lifestyle: what concrete step will I take this week? Relationships: how do I make peace with God, myself and others? Ministry: how will I serve and help build God's system?

You do not need all five every time, but move from the inside out. Lasting change in behaviour begins with a changed mindset. Demanding outward behaviour without touching the inner mindset is like tying fruit onto a dead tree: it looks fruitful, but there is no life.

secs.h: 3. Specific, Doable, Time-Bound
p: “We should love people more” is a direction, not an application. A good application is specific: “This week, pray three times for a colleague you find difficult, and buy them a coffee.” It is doable for an ordinary listener. And it has a time: today, this week, this month.

Remember different listeners: long-time believers, new believers, those not yet believing, and those who are suffering. A sermon has one big idea, yet it can offer different people different next steps.

secs.h: 4. Application Flows From Grace
p: Application easily slides into legalism: “You should, you must, you're not good enough.” The gospel order is: because Christ has already accomplished it for you, you can live like this. We do good not in order to be saved but because we have been saved.

The old self-centred life cannot do it; only the new self-emptied life can. So every application must finally bring people back to the cross and resurrection: “I can do all things through Christ who strengthens me” (Philippians 4:13).

c321: Change your mindset and you change your life; change your life and you change how you live. The five layers of change are the skeleton of application.
Change begins with me: the preacher must first practise the application himself before he can call others to it with conviction.
act: For your next sermon, write one application each for mindset, life, lifestyle, relationships and ministry, then choose the two most important.
Rewrite each application as a specific, doable, time-bound sentence.
Check the tone of your applications: “Because Christ has… you can,” or “You should…”?
chk: After hearing it, will people know what to do on Monday?
Do my applications move from the inside out, or only demand outward behaviour?
Have I lived this application myself first?
disc: Why do so many sermons move people a lot yet change them little?
Analyse a passage you read recently using the five layers of change.
How do legalistic and gospel-shaped applications sound different?
lessons.pray: Lord, make me not only a hearer but a doer of your word. Use your word as a mirror to shine on me, and through the word I preach shine on the congregation, so that we are renewed from the inside out and live out Christ in daily life. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray, Amen.

lessons.sub: Drawing People In, Leading Them to Respond

key.x: Now when they heard this, they were cut to the heart, and said to Peter and the rest of the apostles, “Brothers, what shall we do?”

lessons.big: The opening opens the door; the closing leads people through it. The best closing makes the congregation ask, “What shall we do?”

secs.h: 1. Opening: The First Two Minutes Decide the Next Thirty
p: When people sit down, their minds are still on parking, children and work. The opening's task is to gather their attention and bring it before God's Word. In Athens Paul began with an altar inscribed “TO AN UNKNOWN GOD” (Acts 17:23), entering the gospel through something familiar to them.

Good openings include a personal question, a short story, a surprising fact or a real-life dilemma. There is only one rule: connect quickly to the big idea. An opening is like a plane taking off — if the runway is too long, the passengers grow restless.

secs.h: 2. What to Avoid in an Opening
p: Avoid long apologies: “I'm not well prepared, I'm not a good speaker…” They drain the congregation's confidence and pull the focus back onto yourself. Avoid jokes unrelated to the topic: after the laughter, no one knows what you are going to say.
Also avoid “starting from Genesis.” Background should be given, but only what the congregation needs. The opening is not about how much you know but how much they need.

secs.h: 3. Closing: Time to Draw the Net
p: Peter's Pentecost sermon closed with a clear call: “Repent and be baptized, every one of you, in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit” (Acts 2:38). That day about three thousand were added.
A closing is not repeating everything again. Strike the big idea once more in its most concentrated sentence, then clearly invite a response. A fisherman who casts the net must finally draw it in.

secs.h: 4. The Spiritual Principles of an Invitation
p: An invitation may be to receive Christ, to repent and confess, to dedicate one's life, to take a concrete step, or to pray in silence. It should be clear, gentle and free of manipulation. We may plead earnestly, but we must not use emotional pressure or guilt to force decisions, because it is the Holy Spirit, not the preacher, who changes hearts.
Close by giving glory to God. The final prayer is not the preacher's summary performance, but leading the congregation together into the Lord's presence so that Jesus may reign in every heart.

c321: Among the eight steps for changing a mindset, “conviction” is followed by “practice.” The invitation at the close helps people step from conviction into practice.
Let Jesus be King: the purpose of an invitation is not to have people follow the preacher but to have them yield to Christ.
act: Write three openings for your sermon (question, story, fact) and choose the one that reaches the big idea fastest.
Condense your big idea into a closing “golden line” of about eight words.
Write a clear, gentle, non-manipulative invitation, followed by a closing prayer.
chk: Does my opening reach the topic within two minutes?
Does my closing contain a clear invitation?
Does my invitation rely on the Holy Spirit or on emotional pressure?
disc: What is the most engaging sermon opening you have heard?
Why did Peter's sermon leave people “cut to the heart”?
Where is the line between an invitation and manipulation?
lessons.pray: Lord, let my openings open the door of people's hearts and my closings lead them into your grace. I do not rely on technique or emotion, only on the power of the Holy Spirit, so that those who hear are cut to the heart, repent and follow you. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray, Amen.

lessons.t: Preaching With the Heart, Relying on the Spirit

key.x: Pray for me, that utterance may be given to me in opening my mouth, to make known with boldness the mystery of the Good News,

lessons.big: Delivery is whole-person worship: when the heart burns first, voice, eyes and body all say the same thing.

secs.h: 1. Even Paul Asked for Prayer
p: The apostle Paul wrote this while in chains. He did not ask for release; he asked the believers to pray “that utterance may be given to me in opening my mouth, to make known with boldness.” Utterance and boldness are not reserved for the naturally gifted; they are grace we can ask for and receive.
So the most important preparation before you go up is having people pray for you. Build a prayer team so that your spiritual companions keep watch in prayer while you preach.

secs.h: 2. Voice: Words With Warmth
p: “Let your speech always be with grace, seasoned with salt” (Colossians 4:6). The voice has four tools: pace, volume, pitch and pause. Slow down at important points; lower the volume where it is tender; lift the pitch where it is stirring; pause for two seconds before and after a key sentence so the words can land.
The pause is the preacher's most underrated tool. In music a rest is also music. Silence gives the congregation room to think and the Holy Spirit room to work.

secs.h: 3. Body: Eyes, Gestures and Stance
p: Eye contact makes people feel you are speaking to them, not reading at them. Divide the room into left, centre and right, and look at different people in turn. Let gestures be natural and match the content; stand steadily, without swaying or pacing.
You may bring notes, but do not be bound by them. Know them well enough that one glance gives you a whole section; then your eyes can lift from the page and see the people.

secs.h: 4. With the Heart, Not the Head
p: Technique is the vessel; the heart is the source. “A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in settings of silver” (Proverbs 25:11). A fitting word comes from a heart filled with the Spirit and full of love for the congregation. Preaching from the head worries about forgetting lines and about performance; preaching from the heart is focused on God and on people.

When you are nervous, move the focus from yourself to Jesus: “Lord, this is your word, your people, your moment.” Use your heart and you find joy; use your head and you find worry. When you know you are carrying the King's message, you can be both bold and at rest.

c321: The path of service, “Life”: Jesus is my example — grow in and live out the life of Jesus, so that even the tone of our voice carries his grace and truth.
Use your heart and rely on the Spirit, not your head and yourself: peace in the pulpit comes from the Spirit's presence, not from polished technique.
act: Record yourself on your phone giving a five-minute message. On playback, listen only to your voice; then watch only your body.
Mark your notes with symbols for “slow down,” “pause” and “emphasise.”
Invite two or three spiritual companions to form your preaching prayer team.
chk: When I preach, are my eyes mostly on my notes or on people?
Does my voice vary, or is it one speed and volume throughout?
Before I go up, is my heart filled with the Spirit or with nerves?
disc: Which preaching habit do you find most distracting?
Why does a pause have power?
How can “boldness” and “rest” exist together?
lessons.pray: Holy Spirit, give me utterance, that I may open my mouth boldly to make known the mystery of the gospel. Cleanse my lips, warm my voice, and let my eyes and body show the love of Christ. I will not use my head and rely on myself, but use my heart and rely on you. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray, Amen.

key.x: Likewise, you younger ones, be subject to the elder. Yes, all of you clothe yourselves with humility and subject yourselves to one another; for “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.”

lessons.big: The end of the sermon is the beginning of growth. Humility is the key to progress; God gives grace to those willing to be corrected.

secs.h: 1. Two Temptations After Preaching
p: When it goes well, the temptation is pride: “I really am gifted.” When it goes badly, the temptation is also pride, just wearing another face: “I'm hopeless; I'll never preach again.” Both have “me” at the centre.

Pride provokes pride, pride fights pride, and both sides lose. Humility draws out humility, humility meets humility, and both sides win. When praised, offer the praise to God; when criticised, treat it as the whetstone God uses to sharpen you.

secs.h: 2. Iron Sharpens Iron: Building Feedback Relationships
p: “Iron sharpens iron; so a man sharpens his friend's countenance” (Proverbs 27:17). Find one or two spiritual companions who love you and dare to tell you the truth, and ask them for regular feedback. Ask specific questions: “Was the big idea clear? Which part helped most? Which part was hard to follow?”

When you receive feedback, say thank you first and do not defend yourself. Even if they are not entirely right, there is often one sentence in it that God wants you to hear. Humility is the key to revival, and the key to growth in preaching.

secs.h: 3. Review With the Eight Steps
p: The 321 vision's eight steps for changing a mindset — information, revelation, conviction, practice, review, correction, repetition, multiplication — are the very cycle of a preacher's growth. After preaching, enter “review”: what went well? What needs improving? Then “correction”: what exactly will I change next time?

Then “repetition”: change one or two things at a time and keep practising. Do not try to fix everything at once; that leads to discouragement. Like learning the piano, master one bar a week and in a year you can play a whole piece.

secs.h: 4. God Is the Final Judge
p: People's evaluation is useful but not final. Paul said, “With me it is a very small thing that I should be judged by you… he who judges me is the Lord” (1 Corinthians 4:3-4). The question we must finally ask is: “Lord, are you pleased? Was I faithful?”

Sometimes an ordinary sermon turns someone back to God; sometimes one we thought excellent shows no visible fruit. The results are in God's hands. Our responsibility is to sow faithfully; it is God who gives the increase.

c321: Humility overcomes pride: God resists the proud and gives grace to the humble. Reviewing after preaching is the most practical place to practise humility.
The eight steps for changing a mindset: review, correction and repetition are the preacher's road from failure to victory.
act: Within 24 hours of preaching, complete a review using this app's “After-Sermon Review” tool.
Invite a spiritual companion to give you feedback with three specific questions; only say thank you, do not defend yourself.
Choose one item from the feedback and work specifically on it next time.
chk: When praised, do I give the glory to God?
When criticised, do I become defensive or discouraged?
Do I have spiritual companions who regularly tell me the truth?
disc: Why is discouragement after a poor sermon actually a form of pride?
How can we give a preacher feedback that is both honest and edifying?
How does “he who judges me is the Lord” set a preacher free?
lessons.pray: Lord, I want to clothe myself with humility. When praised, let me lay the crown at your feet; when criticised, let me be teachable before you. Use my brothers and sisters to sharpen me, so that each time I become more useful to you. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray, Amen.

lessons.sub: Letting Jesus Receive All the Glory

key.x: If anyone speaks, let it be as it were the very words of God. If anyone serves, let it be as of the strength which God supplies, that in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ, to whom belong the glory and the dominion forever and ever. Amen.

lessons.big: The goal of preaching is not one good sermon but building God's system: raising more people to speak God's Word, so that God is glorified in all things.

secs.h: 1. As the Very Words of God
p: Peter says, “If anyone speaks, let it be as it were the very words of God.” This sentence sums up the whole course. What we speak is not our own opinion but God's Word; we rely not on our own strength but on the strength God supplies; the aim is not our own glory but “that in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ.”
This is the path of service in five words: Spirit, Understanding, Life, Serve, God. The Spirit guides, we grasp the truth, live out the life, serve in the Lord, and give the glory to God.

secs.h: 2. Four Generations of Passing It On
p: Paul told Timothy, “The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit the same things to faithful men who will be able to teach others also” (2 Timothy 2:2). There are four generations here: Paul, Timothy, faithful men, and others. The gift of preaching is not a treasure to hoard but a torch to pass on.

One preacher can preach only so many sermons in a lifetime. But if he trains ten preachers, and each trains ten more, the voice of the gospel multiplies. This is the last of the eight steps: multiplication.

secs.h: 3. Training Preachers in 235 Relationships
p: The best environment for multiplying preachers is the 235 spiritual relationships: among your 2 spiritual companions, pray for and give feedback to one another; in 3 spiritual parent-child relationships, lead newcomers to share a testimony first, then lead a Bible study, then give a short message; in the 5 team of fivefold ministry co-workers, serve together according to each one's gifts.

The practical steps: I do, you watch; I do, you help; you do, I help; you do, I watch; then you go and train someone else. That is how Jesus trained his disciples — first living with them, then sending them out.

secs.h: 4. Crowns Before the Throne
p: Revelation records that the twenty-four elders “throw their crowns before the throne” (Revelation 4:10). All of a preacher's sermons, all the fruit and all the praise of a lifetime will finally be laid before the Lord's throne. “I planted. Apollos watered. But God gave the increase” (1 Corinthians 3:6).

This is the destination of 321 preaching: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory, and build God's system. May you become a victorious preacher who raises up more victorious preachers, pressing toward the great revival of the last days and the return of the Lord Jesus.

c321: One purpose: build God's system. Preachers multiplying preachers is extending the territory of God's kingdom on earth.
Two cores: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory. Everything is what God has done and accomplished in Jesus; all of it is God's grace.
act: Name one “Timothy” you can begin to train, and pray for them for a week.
Invite them to share a three-minute testimony in your small family group, and give encouraging feedback.
Write a thank-you letter to the spiritual parent who trained you to preach, and offer what you have learned in this course to the Lord.
chk: Is my gift of preaching building up myself or building up others?
Is there a preacher I am currently training?
Do I give the glory to God in all things?
disc: How could the four generations of 2 Timothy 2:2 be practised in your church or small family group?
“I do, you watch; I do, you help; you do, I help; you do, I watch” — which step do you most often get stuck on?
Looking back over the twelve lessons, which one most changed your view of preaching?
lessons.pray: Lord of glory, I lay everything I have learned in this course before your throne. Make me speak as the very words of God and serve in the strength you supply, and use me to train more faithful preachers. May you be glorified in all things through Jesus Christ, forever and ever. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray, Amen.

lessons.t: The Truth Meal-Kit Method of Preaching
lessons.sub: God, People and AI Working Together

key.x: but to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God.

lessons.big: God is God, people are people, AI is a tool. Get the order right and everything falls into place. A truth meal-kit is only half-made: first pour in the pure living water of the Spirit, then heat it with faith, add your testimony and season it with the Spirit's prompting, and it becomes bread of life for others.

secs.h: 1. Three Kinds of Wisdom: Source, Receiver, Helper
p: When people hear “AI” and “preaching” together, some are excited: “Finally, AI can write my sermons!” Some are worried: “Can a sermon written by AI still carry the Spirit's prompting?” Some refuse: “Preaching is the Spirit's work; AI has no place in it!” Each reaction has a point, yet each sees only part of the truth. We are not replacing the Holy Spirit with AI, nor rejecting every new tool. Under God's guidance we use the tools he allows in this age to pass on truth and build lives more effectively.

There are three kinds of wisdom. Christ is the wisdom of God, the source of all wisdom. We are “God-made intelligence”: people God created and works in, the receivers. AI is “artificial intelligence”: a tool made by people, the helper. Source, receiver, helper — this order must never be reversed.

It is like water flowing from a mountain spring: first into the river (people), then into irrigation channels (tools), finally watering the fields (the congregation's lives). The spring decides the quality of the water. If the source is God's Word and the Spirit's guidance, the water stays clean through every channel. If the source is polluted, however advanced the channels, what flows out is still dirty water.

secs.h: 2. God's Wisdom: Christ Is the Source of All Truth
p: Paul declares that “Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24). Christ does not merely have wisdom; he is wisdom itself. To Corinth, a city that prized Greek philosophy, Paul said: the wisdom you seek is not in the halls of philosophy but at the cross.

In Christ “all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden” (Colossians 2:3). Insights from science, management, communication and psychology, if they are true, finally point to Christ. AI can process vast information, quote verses and arrange theology, yet it does not know Christ, cannot receive the Spirit's revelation and cannot experience a relationship with God. Cut off from the source, all wisdom is only fragments.

secs.h: 3. God-Made Intelligence: We Are His Workmanship
p: “For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared before that we would walk in them” (Ephesians 2:10). The Greek word poiēma is the root of the English word “poem.” You are God's poem, his masterpiece — not a product off an assembly line, but a work made by the Master's own hand.

AI is artificial, trained with data and algorithms; you are God-made, shaped by his Spirit, his Word and every experience of your life. AI can write a grammatically perfect sermon, but it cannot weep; it can list a hundred analogies, but it cannot say “I have lived this.” You have three things AI will never have: life, experience and the Holy Spirit. Preaching is not passing on information but sharing life.

secs.h: 4. Artificial Intelligence: A Tool, Not a Master
p: AI can organise knowledge, search verses and commentaries, draft outlines, polish wording and make slides. But it cannot replace the Spirit's guidance, cannot pray for you to seek God's heart, cannot touch lives with a life, and cannot discern “what the Spirit wants to say to these people right now.”

AI is like a sharp knife: in the kitchen it makes a beautiful meal; in surgery it saves lives; but if you let the knife decide what you do, you are in danger. The Bible is my standard; AI is not. Everything AI produces must be tested by Scripture: keep what agrees with the Bible, firmly discard what does not. A tool is a tool; the master is the master.

secs.h: 5. Working Together: Order and Three Red Lines
p: The right way to work together is: God guides people, people guide AI, AI does the work. First receive through prayer, Scripture and the Spirit's prompting the core message God wants you to bring. Then, with that direction, ask AI to gather background, illustrations and data. Finally AI organises and carries out your instructions. It is like building the temple: God gave the plan, Solomon led the craftsmen to follow it, and the craftsmen built with tools. Tools matter, but they can never matter more than the plan.

This is the 321 principle of letting people be people and God be God: God is God, people are people, AI is a tool. There are three red lines. People must not replace God — “Trust in the LORD with all your heart, and don't lean on your own understanding” (Proverbs 3:5). AI must not replace people — never read an AI-written sermon straight from the page; the congregation can tell whether you are sharing your life or reading someone else's script. And AI must never replace God — when you rely on AI to tell you what to preach instead of relying on the Spirit, AI has already taken God's place. Within these lines, use the tools freely and boldly; beyond them is danger.

“A craftsman who wants to do good work first sharpens his tools,” says an old Chinese proverb. David used a sling, Paul used letters, and the printing press spread the Bible widely. It has been said that AI will not replace people, but people who use AI will replace those who don't. Yet using AI is not the same as depending on AI: the first is using a tool well; the second is being used by the tool.

secs.h: 6. What Is a Truth Meal-Kit?
p: A supermarket meal-kit has the ingredients cut and portioned, so you don't start from scratch — but you still cook it, season it and judge the heat yourself. A truth meal-kit is the same: the Spirit guides you to the theme, you use AI to gather material, and it is assembled into a kit of slides, a manuscript, verses, illustrations and applications. It saves you hours of research, but it cannot preach for you.

A complete kit has six ingredients: first, biblical truth — key and related passages, original language, background and theology, the main ingredient; second, the Spirit's revelation — what you receive in your own time with God, which AI cannot produce; third, the 321 vision — three foundations, two cores, one purpose, helping people live it out; fourth, knowledge — psychology, brain science, management and history that support the truth; fifth, illustrations — making truth concrete, felt and remembered; sixth, life application — concrete steps people can take afterwards.

One kit can become many forms: slides, a manuscript (for internalising, not for reading aloud), key-line cards, one-to-three-minute short videos, and podcasts. A sermon is no longer only forty minutes on Sunday; it can keep shaping lives all week.

secs.h: 7. The Four Adds: Add Water, Heat It, Add to It, Season It
p: The kit is not the finished dish; the preacher must cook it, with four “adds” — and the first is water. Add water — the pure living water of the Holy Spirit. A meal-kit is dry and concentrated; without water it cannot be cooked or dissolved. Jesus said, “He who believes in me, as the Scripture has said, from within him will flow rivers of living water.” But he said this about the Spirit (John 7:38-39). Adding water means asking to be filled with the Spirit and cleansed through confession before you prepare and before you go up, and relying on the Spirit's presence and anointing as you speak, so that living water flows from within. This water must be pure, unmixed with our pride, performance or human agenda — only when self is laid down can living water flow. The water is what the Spirit himself pours out, so it comes first; with living water the other three adds can cook, and the whole message comes alive and refreshes those who hear.

Heat it by mixing truth with faith: “the word they heard didn't profit them, because it wasn't mixed with faith by those who heard” (Hebrews 4:2). Be moved by the truth yourself first; don't only study the text, soak in it. Augustine is often quoted: “In you must burn what you wish to kindle in others.”

Add to it with your own testimony: “They overcame him because of the Lamb's blood, and because of the word of their testimony” (Revelation 12:11). One or two real stories carry more power than ten pages of theory, because people connect with life, not information. Life first, then relationships, then ministry — preaching without life is noise; preaching with life is music.

Season it with the Spirit's personal prompting. A “good sermon” is accurate and well structured; a “right sermon” is what the Spirit wants to say to these people now. Keep asking the Spirit, “What else would you add? What should I emphasise?” And don't fill every minute — leave space for the Spirit to speak.

secs.h: 8. Internalising the Truth and the Preaching Flow
p: After the four adds, internalise it so the kit becomes your own message: read it thoroughly to grasp its flow; meditate — “his delight is in the LORD's law. On his law he meditates day and night” (Psalm 1:2); receive, writing down the fresh angles the Spirit gives; arrange it in your own words and rhythm; and let it become your own message, so that in the pulpit you share what you have digested and lived.

Preaching is not reading a script or performing; it is sharing life. Paul said they were “well pleased to impart to you not the Good News of God only, but also our own souls” (1 Thessalonians 2:8). Being without self is not emptiness; it is letting Christ live in you.

The full flow: begin with prayer — not by switching on the computer; deliver the message — looking at people, not at the slides; give an invitation — truth is meant to be answered; allow a time of response in prayer — giving the Spirit room to work deeply; close with a blessing — “The LORD bless you, and keep you. The LORD make his face to shine on you, and be gracious to you. The LORD lift up his face toward you, and give you peace” (Numbers 6:24-26).

c321: The three foundations matter even more in the age of AI: the Holy Spirit is my guide — the starting point is always the Spirit's guidance, not AI output; the Bible is my standard — everything AI produces must be tested by Scripture; Jesus is my example — preaching is sharing the life of Christ in me.

The path of service: Spirit → Understanding → Life → Serve → God. AI can help you organise, arrange and polish, but it cannot pray for you, seek the Spirit for you or live your life for you. Let people be people, let God be God, and let AI be a tool.
act: For your next sermon, first pray for the theme, then use this app's “Truth Meal-Kit Workshop” to ask Xiaozhi for ingredients, and test every item against Scripture.

First “add water” to this message — ask to be filled with the Spirit and cleansed, so living water can flow from within; then “add to” it: write a short testimony of how God has led you (one or two paragraphs).
Before preaching, take the five steps of internalising — read, meditate, receive, arrange, make it your own — and leave a space in the sermon for the Holy Spirit.
chk: Do I open the Bible and kneel in prayer first, or open AI first?
Does this sermon contain my own testimony and the Spirit's prompting, or only material AI has gathered?
Am I preaching in the Spirit's living water, or relying on notes and technique? Is my heart mixed with pride or performance?
Have I crossed any of the three red lines: people replacing God, AI replacing people, AI replacing God?
Am I using the tool, or is the tool using me?
disc: “God is God, people are people, AI is a tool” — which part of this order is most easily reversed in your ministry?
How do you test whether AI-provided content agrees with Scripture? Give an example.
Of the four adds — add water, heat it, add to it, season it — which do you most need to practise? Why?
lessons.pray: Dear Father, thank you for the new tools you have given in our time. Help us come to you before we use any tool — to pray first, listen first and receive first. Let the Holy Spirit always be our guide, the Bible always our standard and Jesus always our example. Guard our hearts so that we do not rely on tools and neglect you, nor reject tools and miss your provision. Let every sermon that begins with a truth meal-kit be filled first with the pure living water of the Spirit, then warmed by our lives and seasoned by the Spirit, becoming bread of life that feeds souls. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray, Amen.

tools: Spirit · Understanding · Life · Serve · God — nine steps to a sermon
God guides people, people guide AI, AI does the work
A heart and practical check before you preach
Review, correct and repeat with the eight steps
Time each section and keep your pace

bsteps.h: Don't open a commentary yet. Read the passage three times quietly before the Lord and ask the Spirit, “What do you want to say to me and the congregation through this today?” Write down the first prompting.
f: The Spirit's first prompting to me

bsteps.h: Who? When? Where? What happened? Watch for repeated words, connectives (because, therefore, but), commands and promises. The more detailed, the better.
Look at the context, the theme of the book, the background, and let Scripture interpret Scripture. A passage has one original meaning but many applications. How does it point to Christ?
f: How the passage points to Christ

bsteps.h: In one sentence (about 25 words) say what the text says and therefore how we respond. Try shifting from the human view to God's, earthly to heavenly, temporary to eternal, worldly to godly.
f: Shift of viewpoint: people see… God sees…
How has this truth changed me first?

bsteps.h: Two to four points, parallel in form, about eight words each, all directly supporting the big idea. Under each: state, illustrate, apply.
An illustration is a window, not the house: clear, fitting, close to life, true. The hero of a testimony is Jesus, not me.
f: My testimony (how the Lord helped me)

bsteps.h: Inside out: mindset → life → lifestyle → relationships → ministry. Specific, doable, time-bound; flowing from grace: “Because Christ has done it, you can…”
f: Mindset: which thought must be renewed?
Life: which quality of Christ should grow?
Lifestyle: what concrete step this week?
Relationships: peace with God, self and others?
Ministry: how to serve and build God's system?

bsteps.h: Reach the big idea within two minutes; close by striking it once more in a golden line, then invite a response clearly, gently, without manipulation.
Place the sermon in the Lord's hands. Write the closing prayer, and a “crown-laying prayer” for yourself before you go up. End with “in the name of the Lord Jesus we pray, Amen.”
f: Crown-laying prayer: Lord, this is your…
